title: Terrorism and Nuclear Proliferation

cards.h: Two threats that touch India directly
cards.b:
Terrorism and nuclear weapons are the two security issues that bring global politics closest to India's borders. India faces cross-border terrorism from Pakistan and is surrounded by nuclear-armed neighbours, China and Pakistan.

Both topics also test the international order. There is no agreed UN definition of terrorism. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) has been called discriminatory, and its 2026 review conference ended without agreement.

Expect questions that ask you to compare the global response with India's stand, to assess the NPT regime, and to link nuclear policy to deterrence (see the lesson on balance of power and deterrence).

Learn the dates. Terrorism: 1999 Resolution 1267, 2001 Resolution 1373, 2006 Global Strategy. Nuclear: 1968 NPT, 1996 CTBT, 1998 Pokhran-II, 2008 civil nuclear waiver, 2026 New START expiry and NPT RevCon.

cards.h: What is terrorism? The definition problem
cards.b:
Terrorism is violence or the threat of it against civilians, used to spread fear and push a political goal. Bruce Hoffman's Inside Terrorism (1998) stresses that it is political, aims at psychological effect and is carried out by a group or network.

But there is no agreed legal definition at the UN. Disputes: whether to include state action, and whether to exempt "freedom struggles" against occupation. "One person's terrorist is another's freedom fighter" is the common quip.

India proposed a Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism (CCIT) in 1996. It remains stuck in the General Assembly's Sixth Committee.

Forms of terrorism

  • Home-grown, and cross-border or state-sponsored.
  • Religious, ethno-nationalist, left-wing, right-wing.
  • Lone-wolf, cyber and online radicalisation.
  • Use of drones and cryptocurrency for financing.

David Rapoport's "four waves" (2004) of modern terrorism: anarchist (1880s), anti-colonial, new left, and religious (from 1979).

cards.h: From 9/11 to ISIS and the Taliban's return
cards.b:
• 11 September 2001. Al-Qaeda's attacks on the US. The US launched the "war on terror" and invaded Afghanistan in October 2001. The Iraq war followed in 2003.
  • 2014. The Islamic State (ISIS) declared a "caliphate" in Iraq and Syria. It was territorially defeated by 2019 but its franchises continue in Africa and Asia.
  • August 2021. The Taliban retook Kabul after the US withdrawal. Concerns grew over groups like Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed finding space.
  • Africa's Sahel has become a leading region for deadly attacks in recent years.

Robert Pape's Dying to Win (2005) argued that suicide attacks respond mostly to foreign military occupation, not religion alone. Huntington's "clash of civilizations" thesis (1993; book 1996) is the contrary frame often cited.

Scholars debate whether the war on terror made the world safer, or whether it fuelled radicalisation (Iraq, Guantanamo).

UN Security Council

  • Resolution 1267 (1999) and successors: a sanctions regime on the Taliban, then Al-Qaeda and ISIL. The list freezes assets and bans travel and arms. Listing of Masood Azhar (Jaish-e-Mohammed) was blocked by China's "technical hold" for years until it was listed on 1 May 2019.
  • Resolution 1373 (2001), passed after 9/11, binds all states to criminalise terror financing and deny safe haven. It set up the Counter-Terrorism Committee.

Other pieces

  • UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy (2006), with four pillars including root causes, prevention and human rights. The UN Office of Counter-Terrorism was set up in 2017.
  • FATF (1989) sets rules on money-laundering and terror financing. Pakistan was on its grey list from 2018 to October 2022.
  • Regional: SCO's RATS, the Global Counterterrorism Forum, the Quad, BRICS and G20 statements.

Gaps: no definition, politicised listings, vetoes, and uneven action against state sponsors.

India has been a target for decades: the 2001 Parliament attack, the Mumbai attacks of 26 November 2008 (26/11), Uri (2016) and Pulwama (2019).

India's doctrine in action

  • 2016: after Uri, "surgical strikes" across the Line of Control (29 September).
  • 2019: after Pulwama, an air strike at Balakot (26 February).
  • 2025: after the Pahalgam attack (22 April), India launched Operation Sindoor on 7 May. A ceasefire followed on 10 May. India declared that terror attacks would be treated as acts of war and that it would not distinguish between terrorists and their sponsors.
  • Law. UAPA (1967, amended 2004, 2008, 2019), NIA Act 2008 (after 26/11), and NATGRID.
  • Diplomacy. Calls for the CCIT; "zero tolerance"; pressure at FATF and the UN; extradition of 26/11 accused Tahawwur Rana from the US (April 2025).
  • Indus Waters Treaty placed in abeyance (April 2025) as a lever, a move Pakistan rejects.

Critics ask about the escalation risk between two nuclear-armed states, and whether deterrence by punishment works.

The NPT opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. It was extended indefinitely in 1995. It has about 190 parties.

  • The five nuclear-weapon states (NWS) are those that tested before 1 January 1967. They promise not to help others get weapons and to pursue disarmament (Article VI).
  • All others promise not to acquire them, in return for access to peaceful nuclear technology (Article IV), under IAEA safeguards.
  • Outside: India, Pakistan, Israel (undeclared) and South Sudan. North Korea announced withdrawal in 2003 and has tested since 2006.

Review conferences are held every five years. The 2015, 2022 and 2026 conferences all ended without a consensus final document. The 2026 one (27 April to 22 May) broke down mainly over Iran.

cards.h: The wider regime and arms control
cards.b:
• CTBT (1996): bans all nuclear test explosions. It is not in force, as key states (the US, China, and others, plus India, Pakistan and North Korea) have not ratified. India has not signed.
  • FMCT: a proposed ban on producing fissile material. Talks are stuck at the Conference on Disarmament.
  • Export controls: the Nuclear Suppliers Group (1975, born after India's 1974 test), the MTCR (1987), the Wassenaar Arrangement and the Australia Group. India joined the MTCR (2016), Wassenaar (2017) and the Australia Group (2018), but not the NSG, where China resists.
  • Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (2017, in force January 2021). Nuclear states and their allies, India included, stay out.
  • Nuclear-weapon-free zones such as Tlatelolco (Latin America) and Rarotonga.

US-Russia arms control is unravelling

The ABM Treaty ended in 2002 and the INF Treaty in 2019. New START (2010), the last limit on strategic forces, expired on 5 February 2026, leaving no treaty cap for the first time in decades.

• Iran. The 2015 JCPOA limited its programme. The US left it in 2018. Israel and the US struck Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025, and fighting broke out again from 28 February 2026. IAEA access has been badly limited, and Iranian lawmakers have talked of leaving the NPT. The situation remains fluid, so check the latest.
  • North Korea. Six nuclear tests between 2006 and 2017. It has ballistic missiles and rejects denuclearisation.
  • Pakistan. Its programme grew with help from the A.Q. Khan network, which also supplied Libya, Iran and North Korea.
  • Success stories. South Africa gave up its bombs (1989-91). Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan returned Soviet weapons after 1991. Libya gave up its programme in 2003.

Ukraine's loss of territory after giving up weapons (the 1994 Budapest Memorandum) is cited by some as a lesson that giving up weapons is risky. The Budapest Memorandum gave assurances, not a binding guarantee.

Theory. Kenneth Waltz ("The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: More May Be Better", 1981) held that more nuclear states can bring stability through deterrence. Scott Sagan (the Sagan-Waltz debate, 1995) replied that organisational accidents and bad decisions make spread dangerous.

The case against the NPT

It divides the world into nuclear "haves" and "have-nots" by a date (1967), creating what India called nuclear apartheid. The five powers have not met Article VI, and modernise their arsenals. Enforcement is selective: friends such as Israel face no penalty, while rivals face sanctions.

The case for it

Without it, many more states might have the bomb. John F. Kennedy once feared 15 to 25 nuclear states by the 1970s. Today there are nine. The NPT set a strong norm (the "nuclear taboo", Nina Tannenwald, 2007).

Wider questions

Does deterrence keep peace or risk catastrophe? Is a world without nuclear weapons realistic? The TPNW says yes, nuclear states say no. Nuclear dangers also rise with new technology: hypersonic weapons, AI in command systems, and weak limits in space and cyber.

• 1974. Pokhran-I, a "peaceful nuclear explosion". The NSG was created in response.
  • 1998. Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti, 11 and 13 May). India declared itself a nuclear-weapon state. Pakistan tested on 28 and 30 May.
  • Doctrine. Draft doctrine in 1999; the Cabinet Committee on Security approved the operational framework in January 2003: credible minimum deterrence, no first use (against nuclear weapons, but with a right to respond to chemical or biological attack), massive retaliation if attacked, and civilian control through the Nuclear Command Authority.
  • India-US civil nuclear deal. The 123 Agreement (signed October 2008). The NSG gave India a waiver on 6 September 2008, and India agreed on safeguards for its civilian reactors.
  • Positions. India has long called for universal, time-bound disarmament (the Rajiv Gandhi Action Plan, 1988), but refuses to join the NPT as a non-nuclear state or sign the CTBT. It keeps a voluntary moratorium on testing.

After Operation Sindoor, India's leaders said they would not accept "nuclear blackmail".

"Discuss the challenges to the global nuclear non-proliferation regime. How has India dealt with them?"
"Examine the NPT as a discriminatory regime."
"Terrorism is the greatest challenge to global peace, yet the world has not defined it." Discuss.
"Evaluate India's response to cross-border terrorism."

Structure for terrorism: the definition problem and CCIT; forms; UN framework (1267, 1373, 2006 Strategy), FATF; limits (vetoes, state sponsors); India's response (laws, strikes, diplomacy).

Structure for nuclear: NPT bargain and three pillars; wider regime (CTBT, NSG, TPNW); the unravelling of arms control (New START ended); hotspots (Iran, North Korea); critiques; India's doctrine, 2008 waiver, and the way forward (dialogue, risk reduction).

quiz.w: Binding under Chapter VII; it set up the Counter-Terrorism Committee.

quiz.q: India's draft Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism was proposed in:
quiz.w: India proposed the CCIT in 1996; it remains stalled.

quiz.q: Masood Azhar was listed under the UNSC 1267 regime on:
quiz.w: China lifted its technical hold in 2019.

quiz.q: The Pakistan-focused FATF grey list period ran:
quiz.w: Pakistan was grey-listed in 2018 and removed in October 2022.
After the Pahalgam attack on 22 April 2025.

quiz.q: The five NPT nuclear-weapon states are those that tested before:
Which state announced withdrawal from the NPT in 2003?
quiz.w: North Korea announced withdrawal in January 2003.

quiz.q: The Nuclear Suppliers Group was formed in response to:
quiz.w: Pokhran-I (1974) led to the NSG in 1975.

quiz.q: New START, the last US-Russia limit on strategic nuclear forces, expired on:
quiz.w: It expired on 5 February 2026, after Russia ended compliance and no extension was agreed.

o: Credible minimum deterrence and no first use
quiz.w: Along with massive retaliation and civilian control through the Nuclear Command Authority.
